rows: Grey-headed and black flying foxes resolve about 4 cycles per degree to your 60, a fifteenth of yours and nearly seven times an insect-eating bat’s.
Flying foxes make no echolocation calls and find their way by sight and smell.
Flying foxes have two cone types, a blue and a green, as most mammals do. Cones are about one in two hundred of their light receptors, so colour is muted here.
Rousettes, epauletted fruit bats and the genus of the straw-coloured fruit bat have only the green cone and see no colour. The picture follows the flying foxes.
Bats pack 300,000 to 800,000 rods into each square millimetre of retina, two to five times your densest. Shadows are lifted to suggest it.
The gene for the blue cone of the Formosan flying fox points to ultraviolet. No phone records it, and none is drawn.
Rousette fruit bats echolocate with tongue clicks and land on targets as well as calling bats do, and the picture draws no echoes.
These are guesses, and the camera’s field is kept.
docs/views/sheets/bat.md#2 flyingfox: Field, focus and pupil

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and you see much less fine detail than that. If you are a black, gray-headed or little red flying fox, counts of nerve cells in your eye put your sharpness at between 4 and 6 cycles a degree, a fifth of a human's or less. If you are a Madagascan rousette, the estimate is about 3, roughly a tenth of a human's.

cites.taxon: Pteropus alecto; P. poliocephalus; Rousettus aegyptiacus

rows.note: Gray-headed has two figures (about 4 in R1, 5.5 in R3), so I gave a 4 to 6 range. I left out the Egyptian rousette, because R1 lists it but its quote does not state a value for it.

rows.title: No calls
rows.text: Some bats fly through the dark by sending calls out of the mouth and listening for the echoes. In a flight room, these bats narrowed the beam of their calls when they entered a confined space, and widened it again within dozens of milliseconds when they flew toward open space. Nobody has measured whether you find your way with calls like these.
rows.note: R1 covers mouth-emitting bats in general and says nothing about flying foxes, so I left out any claim that flying foxes do or do not echolocate.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a Madagascan flying fox, a Greater Mascarene flying fox or a Pteropus rodricensis, you have two kinds of cone, mostly for middle-to-long wavelengths and a few for short wavelengths, which gives you the potential for two-color vision. A rousette, an Eidolon and an Epomophorus fruit bat, each measured in one species, have only the long-wavelength kind and are color blind. Nobody has measured which colors the cones in your eyes sense best.

cites.taxon: Pteropus rufus, P. niger, P. rodricensis
Rousettus madagascariensis, Eidolon dupreanum, Epomophorus gambianus

rows.note: Left out R5 (a predicted 360 nm peak in one Pteropus, partial, grade i) and R4 (bats other than Pteropus), since neither measures a flying fox's cone peaks.

rows.title: One cone
rows.text: In the Madagascan rousette, the Madagascan fruit bat and the Gambian epauletted fruit bat, the retina has one kind of cone, the L-cone, and no S-cones at all, which the researchers describe as color blindness. Nobody has measured the cones of the other flying foxes, such as the straw-colored fruit bat, so for them it is not known whether you have one kind too.

cites.taxon: Rousettus madagascariensis, Eidolon dupreanum, Epomophorus gambianus

rows.note: Graded i for the view; R1 measures only three species, so relatives like Egyptian rousette are not stated as carried.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: Nobody has measured the dimmest light you can see, in any flying fox or fruit bat. The only bat measured so far is Daubenton's bat, a small insect-eating bat that is not a close relative of yours, so its figure stays with it.
rows.note: Only record is a Myotis (different family), so I left out its threshold number; it cannot carry to flying foxes.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In eight bat species, pigments made in a lab for the ultraviolet-sensing cell peak at about 360 nanometers, and a review lists the same peak, predicted from its gene, for the flying fox Pteropus samoensis. You very likely have this pigment too, but nobody has measured how far into the ultraviolet you see.
rows.note: R1 does not name its eight species, so I could not say whether any is a flying fox. R2 is a gene-based prediction. No record gives a spectral range.

rows.title: Clicks
rows.text: In a field and flight-room study, bats that send out sound from the mouth narrowed their sound beam when they entered a confined space and widened it again within a few dozen milliseconds when they flew toward open space. Nobody has measured whether you use sound in this way.
rows.note: No record covers Rousettus echolocation, so R1 (mouth-emitting bats) is stated only for those bats and the row says plainly that it is unmeasured in you.
